questions.question: Why does an AI agent that works in demos fail once real users touch it?
questions.answer_summary: Demos are built and tested on clean, curated 'happy path' inputs; real users introduce typos, all-caps text, ambiguous phrasing, and even prompt injection attempts that the agent was never exposed to during development.

questions.question: What are the most common failure modes of AI agents in production?
questions.answer_summary: Documented failure modes include picking the wrong tool (e.g., a hotel-booking API when asked about hiking trails), hallucinating tools that don't exist, answering confidently without calling any tool, and getting stuck in repeat-call loops.

questions.question: Why do external API dependencies cause agents to fail?
questions.answer_summary: Third-party APIs are unreliable in practice - a flight search that should take 3 seconds can take 30, causing the agent to time out and either hallucinate a result or retry until the user gives up.

questions.question: What happens when a tool returns incomplete data to the agent?
questions.answer_summary: If the agent doesn't recognize that returned data is incomplete, it will still pick the 'best' available option from what is effectively a bad menu, producing a confidently wrong answer.

questions.question: Is the root problem the underlying model, or something else?
questions.answer_summary: Multiple practitioner write-ups argue the model itself usually isn't the bottleneck - the real gap is missing planning, missing guardrails, and inadequate testing for messy real-world conditions.

questions.question: What does it take for an AI agent to be considered 'production-ready' rather than a toy?
questions.answer_summary: HN discussion converges on needing persistent memory across sessions, real tool use with error recovery, multi-model support, an extensibility/plugin system, the ability to run as a long-lived service, and security boundaries like sandboxing, permission models, and audit logs.

questions.question: What percentage of agents that are attempted actually make it to reliable production use?
questions.answer_summary: A widely-discussed HN thread framed this directly as 'what makes 5% of AI agents work in production,' reflecting a broad practitioner sense that only a small fraction survive the transition (exact figure not independently verified beyond the discussion framing).

questions.question: Why can't teams just prompt their way out of these failures?
questions.answer_summary: Practitioners argue that prompting harder doesn't fix structural issues like unreliable tool outputs, missing error recovery, or adversarial/messy input - those require engineering (validation, fallback logic, testing), not better wording.

questions.question: How should teams test agents before shipping to avoid these failures?
questions.answer_summary: One practitioner built a YAML-based evaluation framework to check required tool calls happen, cost thresholds aren't exceeded, and behavior stays consistent - reporting ten consecutive incident-free deploys after adopting it.

questions.question: Are most 'agentic' products today actually just read-only RAG rather than true agents?
questions.answer_summary: An HN commenter observed that most agentic demos are effectively fancy read-only retrieval systems, and that real usefulness (e.g., in operational settings) requires giving the agent actual write-access to take action, which introduces its own safety/trust problems.
